title: Question-First Learning Scaffold
problem: Asking a model to 'explain X' produces lecture-style content dumps that don't match how learners actually get stuck. Lessons land better when they're designed around the sequence of questions a real beginner would ask, not the logical structure an expert would use to explain the topic.

workflow.detail: Write one sentence describing what the learner can DO after this lesson — not what they'll 'understand' or 'know'.
Ask the model for the sequence of questions a genuine beginner would ask, moving from confusion toward competence.
Reorder or cut questions based on what actually confuses your real audience — the model's default ordering is a starting guess, not ground truth.

workflow.step: 4. Answer each question as a micro-lesson
workflow.detail: For each question: a short answer, one concrete example, and one check-for-understanding question. One prompt per question keeps each micro-lesson tight.
Stitch the micro-lessons together and ask the model to write only the connective sentences between them — don't let it pad with new content here.

variables.name: OUTCOME
variables.label: Learning outcome
variables.placeholder: e.g. Choose the right one for a given branch situation and do it without fear

variables.name: BACKGROUND
variables.label: Learner background
variables.placeholder: e.g. Comfortable with git add/commit/push, has never touched branching

exampleOutput:
1. **"What's actually different about rebase vs. merge?"** — A merge keeps both histories and adds a merge commit; a rebase replays your commits on top of the other branch, producing a linear history. Example: ... Check: "If you rebase, does the other branch's history change?"
2. **"Why would I ever want a messier merge-commit history?"** — ...

⚠️ Flag: Question 4 assumes familiarity with `git log --graph`, which isn't in the stated background — add a quick primer.
tips: Pilot the question ladder on one real learner before writing full micro-lessons — the first-pass ordering is often wrong.
For slide decks, let each question become one slide title; don't let the model add extra 'context' slides — that's how decks get bloated.
Works well iteratively: when a real learner asks a confused question you didn't anticipate, paste it back in as a new BACKGROUND note to patch the gap.
Keep answers to the stated 2-4 sentences — a question-first scaffold that answers in paragraphs has just become a lecture again.
